summary: Children aged 5–6 learn to read and write numerals 0–20, connecting the spoken number word, the quantity, and the written symbol. This is a foundational symbolic skill requiring numeral recognition on sight, legible numeral formation (a handwriting/motor skill), and two-way mapping between a numeral and a quantity. Teaching keeps numerals tied to amounts, treats digit formation as an explicit motor skill, and directly confronts the teen 'hear-it-write-it' transposition trap (writing 'thirteen' as 31) and classic digit reversals.
misconceptions: Digit reversals (2, 3, 5, 7, 9 written mirror-image) — a formation issue needing direct correction.
Teen transposition from speech: writing 'thirteen' as 31, 'fourteen' as 41 (hearing the ones first).
Reading a numeral without connecting it to a quantity (naming '7' but unable to make seven).
Confusing visually similar numerals (6/9, 2/5, 7/1) or omitting/misreading 0.
Treating a two-digit teen numeral as two separate single digits (reading 15 as 'one, five').

activities.title: Numeral studio: trace, build the quantity, self-correct
steps: Trace a numeral along a guided stroke-order path (start dot and directional arrows) on a whiteboard, in sand, by sky-writing, or on a coded surface that models stroke order.
As the numeral is formed, build or watch a ten-frame fill to that many (using a second ten-frame for 11–20), so the symbol is felt as a quantity rather than a squiggle.
Flip the task: tap/lay out a set of counters, then write or select the numeral that names how many.
Switch frequently between the modes — numeral card → make the set; set → write the numeral; hear it → write it — so reading, writing and representing stay linked.
activities.insight: A numeral is a symbol FOR a quantity, written and read, not a decoration; the three modes (spoken word, quantity, written symbol) are one connected idea.

activities.title: Hear it, write it: addressing the teen transposition
steps: Listen to a spoken teen word, e.g. 'thirteen', and see two ten-frames: one FULL frame of ten and a second frame with 3 more.
Write the numeral by forming the ten digit first and then the ones digit: 1 then 3.
Check: if you write 31, the quantity would need three full tens and one more, which cannot match the single full ten and three extras shown.
Repeat with 'fourteen', 'seventeen', 'nineteen', pairing the spoken word, the ten-structured quantity, and the written numeral each time.
Include 0 deliberately — say 'none', show an empty frame, and read and write the symbol 0.
activities.insight: The words for 13–19 say the ones first ('thir-teen') but the numerals are written ten-then-ones (13); eleven and twelve do not follow this pattern. Pairing the word with a full-ten-plus-extras quantity shows why 13, not 31, is correct.

activities.title: Read-and-match reference wall and checks
steps: Use a 0–20 number track or washing-line pairing each numeral with its position and a matching set; tap or point to a numeral to hear its name and reveal a matching ten-frame display (two frames for 11–20).
Match numeral cards to sets or ten-frames (three-way: numeral ↔ objects ↔ spoken word).
Given a shown or spoken quantity, pick or write the matching numeral, including deliberate 12/21-style distractors to probe the teen trap.
Trace a dictated numeral along a path to check formation.
activities.insight: Recognising and matching numerals to quantities is a distinct, checkable layer that should always reconnect the symbol to an amount and, where possible, to writing it.

checkQuestion: Watch the child read and write. 'Read these: 7, 13, 15, 11, 20. Now write these as I say them: fourteen, seventeen, twelve, nineteen.' Then: 'Here are 16 counters — write how many.' Watch the teens especially.
checkAnswer: Reads all correctly; writes 14, 17, 12, 19; writes 16 for the set — with teens not reversed.
